text:
Newfoundland Court of Appeal

Citation: Farrell v. Canadian
Broadcasting Corporation (No. 1)

Date: 1987-09-18

Docket: 1983 No. 244

Between:

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (Appellant)

and

Thomas Farrell (Respondent)

Goodridge, C.J.N., Gushue, J.A. and Noel, J. (ex
officio)

Counsel:

Ian Kelly, for the appellant;

Peter Alteen, for the respondent.

[
1
]

Gushue, J.A.: This appeal is taken by the
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation ("C.B.C.") from the judgment of
Lang, J., filed November 24, 1983, awarding Thomas Farrell damages in the
amount of $80,000.00 in respect of an acknowledged libel published by C.B.C.
against him. The trial judge also awarded costs on a solicitor and his own
client and on a party and party basis against C.B.C. That order is likewise
appealed: The respondent has cross-appealed on the basis that the damages
awarded are too low.

[
2
]

The facts are as follows: Thomas Farrell is a
medical doctor. At the time relevant to this action (April, 1978) he was not
practicing his profession, but was a member of the Newfoundland House of
Assembly on the Government side. He had been a Cabinet Minister but had
recently relinquished that position. He resided at Apartment 512 of Elizabeth
Towers, a large apartment building in St. John's. On April 26, 1978, a fire occurred
in that apartment, the cause of which was unknown and unexplained. The fire,
while confined to Dr. Farrell's own apartment, necessitated at least partial
evacuation of the building.

[
3
]

An investigation into the fire was carried out
by the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary. Two reports were prepared, the first
dated June 9, 1978 and the second dated July 12, 1978. The authors of the
reports concluded that the fire in apartment 512 had been set by Dr. Farrell.
Copies of the reports were improperly obtained from the Constabulary and
ultimately handed over to the print, television and radio media in St. John's,
including the "Evening Telegram" and the C.B.C. This happened on
September 26, 1978. On September 27 the Evening Telegram published articles in
which Dr. Farrell was named as having been responsible for the fire. Shortly
afterwards, similar stories were broadcast by the C.B.C. on its radio and
television outlets. I shall deal in more detail below with the contents of the
C.B.C. publications, but unquestionably the stories conveyed the impression
that the fire had been set deliberately by Dr. Farrell.

[
4
]

There were various follow-up stories over a
period of five days and in fact, Dr. Farrell was, on October 20, 1978, charged
under
s. 389(1)
of the
Criminal Code of Canada

with having wilfully set
the fire.

[
5
]

Dr. Farrell elected trial by judge and jury. A
preliminary inquiry commenced on December 18, 1978 before Provincial Court
Judge LeClair. On December 21, Dr. Farrell was discharged by Judge LeClair on
the basis of insufficient evidence. The judge later, on February 8, 1979,
delivered written reasons for that discharge.

[
6
]

The matter, however, continued to receive public
attention through various other inquiries and investigations. On February 23,
1979 Judge Soper of the District Court was appointed by the Government under
the
Public Enquiries Act
to determine the circumstances surrounding the
publication of the two police reports. On August 21, 1.979 Judge LeGrow of the
Provincial Court was appointed under the
Summary Jurisdiction Act
to
determine the circumstances surrounding the fire in Dr. Farrell's apartment. In
his report, filed on November 23, 1981, Judge LeGrow concluded that the fire
had in fact been started by Dr. Farrell, accidentally or otherwise. On December
3, 1981 the Minister of Justice requested a legal opinion of the Honourable
R.S. Furlong, retired Chief Justice of Newfoundland, as to whether there was
sufficient evidence to lay a further charge with respect to the fire. That
question was answered in the negative by Chief Justice Furlong.

[
7
]

In the meantime, this action was commenced
against the C.B.C. for libel. Two actions were also taken against the Evening
Telegram. The date of commencement of this action was September 28, 1979. For
various reasons, however, the matter did not actually come to trial until
January 17, 1983. In the meantime the actions against the Evening Telegram had
been tried and judgment was given in the total amount of $150,000.00 by
Mahoney, J., of the Trial Division (as he then was), by way of damages. That
judgment was filed on January 4, 1982. [See:
(1982), 35 Nfld. & P.E.I.R.
181
;
99 A.P.R. 181
.] On May 28, 1982, C.B.C. admitted the libel and broadcast a
full apology to Dr. Farrell. On May 31, 1982 interlocutory judgment was entered
in this matter, by consent, and the C.B.C. paid into court the sum of
$50,000.00 in satisfaction of Dr. Farrell's claim. This was not accepted by Dr.
Farrell and the matter then proceeded to trial before Lang, J. The result of
that trial was the award of $80,000.00 to Dr. Farrell with which we are here
concerned.

[
8
]

Before getting into the reasons for judgment of
the trial judge, it is necessary to set out in some detail the words complained
of and ultimately acknowledged by C.B.C. to have been libellous. These are not
the complete broadcasts, but the gist and extent of the libel may be clearly
gathered from them. Publication occurred in the time period between September
27 and October 5, 1978:

(1)
Interview on "Radio Noon" broadcast - September 27, 1978.

"On April 26 there was a fire in the Elizabeth Towers apartment of Dr. Tom Farrell. It was no ordinary fire. Just the day before
Dr. Farrell had been accused of wrong-doing in a letter tabled in the House of
Assembly. This summer Dr. Farrell resigned his cabinet post after a full
fledged investigation into the spending practices of the Public Works
Department.

"The police were asked to investigate
the Elizabeth Towers fire.' They did and transferred their report to the
Justice Department. Last Thursday, in a copyright story, the St. John's morning
paper, the Daily News, revealed that the report suggests that the fire was
deliberately set and, in fact, named the person suspected of the arson.

"All this poses the question, why
haven't charges been laid.

. . . .
.

"Jim, you report that this report says
that the fire was deliberately set. Do you know who set it?

"Our story said that in the opinion of
the police there was a suspect of that arson and that's all I can say about
that. The police - the report - did give the opinion of the police that they
suspected who set the fire.

. . . .
.

"We checked with our Newsroom. They do,
in fact, have a copy of the police report on the Elizabeth Towers fire. They
received an anonymous phone call yesterday asking if they wanted the report,
and later it was delivered by taxi. The report looks official and it does name
the suspected arsonist who put the match to Dr. Farrell's apartment."

(2)
Item carried on "On The
Go"

radio program - September 27, 1978

"Well, a report prepared by the Nfld.
Constabulary in June named former cabinet minister Dr. Tom Farrell as the one
who started the fire in his Elizabeth Towers apartment. (This has been denied
by Dr. Farrell.) Premier Frank Moores called his cabinet together this
afternoon at 2:30 and that meeting has just ended."

(3)
Extract from 6:00 p.m. radio news - September 27, 1978

"… Here are the highlights of this
evening's news. C.B.C. News has obtained Police documents which named the
suspect in last April's fire at the apartment of Dr. Tom Farrell.

"C.B.C. News has obtained copies of two
of the confidential Police Reports on last April's fire at the apartment of Dr.
Tom Farrell and, as Rick MacInnes–Rae reports, the report quite clearly points
to arson and names the former cabinet minister as the suspect.

"The preliminary reports of the Police
investigation dated June 9 and July 12 are the first in the series of five so
far in the hands of the Justice Department. They have all the stamps, seals,
signatures of police and Justice officials, and the first of them alleges that
the early morning fire was set by Dr. Tom Farrell. That conclusion was drawn by
Detectives Robert Hillier and Sgt. A. Pike who conducted the investigation.
Fire Commissioner John Cardoulis is also named in the report as saying the
blaze was not accidental by incendiary. Specialists stated it was consistent
with the use of an accelerant something to make it burn. It also outlines
contradictions in statements given by Dr. Farrell in police interviews as to
the possible source and cause of the fire and it rules out all possibilities of
an accident. Dr. Farrell himself calls it complete, utter nonsense. The Deputy
Minister of Justice is now studying further reports and he says investigating
officers were not justified in drawing the conclusion of guilt based on the
evidence available. George McAuley also says he is now trying to determine if
there is enough evidence for a case, or whether more investigation is required.

"The Liberal Opposition believes there
may have been a deliberate cover-up in the Elizabeth Towers fire. Opposition
Leader Bill Rowe says if an ordinary citizen were involved the matter would
have been dealt with months ago."

(4)
Extract from regional news on
television program "Here and Now" - September 27, 1978.

(Essentially same as (3) above.

(5)
Interview with investigative reporter
Michael Harris on "Here and Now" program - September 27, 1978.

"Late yesterday copies of the police
investigation of the fire at the apartment of former cabinet minister Dr. Tom
Farrell were made available to all media in St. John's. The reports were
prepared by Det. Robert Hillier for John Kelly, the Director of Public
Prosecutions, and they were dated June 9 and July 12 of this year. The
investigating officer recommended that charges be laid against the occupant,
Dr. Tom Farrell. Here's Michael Harris with more.

. . . .
.

"Months of speculation ended yesterday,
when copies of a police report dated June 9 confirmed that the C.I.D.
investigators had recommended that a charge of arson be laid against former
cabinet minister Dr. Tom Farrell. Here is some of the key statements made by
Det. Robert Hillier in his report to the Director of Public Prosecutions, Mr.
John Kelly.

"Attached are a number of photographs of
the fire scene. Photos show three separate fires and also show deep charring in
three separate areas on the floor of the bedroom of Mr. Farrell. Conclusion: It
has been determined by Mr. Cardoulis, Fire Commissioner; Mr. Spark, special
investigator; Det. Sgt. A. Pike and me that the fire was deliberately set. From
my investigation, it is my opinion and the opinion of Det. Sgt. Pike that the
fire was set by Dr. Farrell. The investigation indicates that Dr. Farrell's
medical problem and the pressure of his work as minister of government have
affected him mentally and it appears that at certain times he becomes
depressed.

"The report stated that several
professional investigators had concluded that the fire was deliberately set.
The experts included two C.I.D. Detectives, Fire Commissioner John Cardoulis
and special investigator Spark of the Insurance Crime Prevention Bureau. Det.
Hillier reported that the fire pattern near Mr. Farrell's bed and fishtailing
in the direction of the doorway was consistent with an accellerant having been used.
An electrician was engaged by the investigators to do a thorough inspection of
the electrical system in Mr. Farrell's apartment, and no electrical malfunction
was found. Carpet samples from the Farrell apartment were tested by Eastern
Technical Services Ltd. to see if a cigarette would ignite them. In the
company's opinion, a lighted cigarette would not cause that type of carpet to
ignite."

(6)
Interview by Harris with John Green,
provincial New Democratic Party leader, on same program.

"Mr. Green, do you believe that there is
a government cover-up in the case of Dr. Tom Farrell?

"Well, I don't know, and that's why we
need more information. That's why it is so crucially important to have the
Minister of Justice or Mr. Browne make a statement either confirming or denying
the report of the fire.

"Well, some of the reports, at least the
last one, named the person who set the fire. The C.I.D. report claimed it was
deliberately set and allegedly names the person who set it. Now this is in the
report that has been leaked, which is of course, an unofficial report. Now if
this is the case we must know immediately what's going on because it seems that
there is a miscarriage of justice here.

"Of course the two reports have been
authenticated by the Police Chief. Chief Browne says in fact they are, in fact,
legitimate reports.

"Well, then, the Minister has no course
but to lay charges or the Chief of Police to lay charges against the person
named by the C.I.D.; because if the C.I.D. named any John Doe for burning down
any ordinary person's house, the normal course of action would be to lay
charges and to arrest the person immediately and promptly. In this case it has
not happened and so there appears to be a miscarriage of justice. There is an
unwarranted delay in making the arrest and the public has a right to know
why."

. . . .
.

(7)
Item from "World at Six"
national C.B.C. radio news - September 27, 1978.

"A former Newfoundland cabinet minister
says he's being disgraced by a police report which accuses him of deliberately
setting a fire in his apartment in St. John's earlier this year. Whit Fraser
reports.

. . . .
.

"Dr. Tom Farrell is furious at police
and the Nfld. Constabulary and newspapers and radio stations in the Province
because details of a police investigation have been made public. The police
report into the fire in his St. John's apartment last April clearly states the
fire was deliberately set. One report completed three months ago was written by
Det. Robert Hillier. It goes on to say it is his opinion and the opinion of
Det. Pike that the fire was set by Dr. Farrell. There is a suggestion that
charges ought to be laid under
Section 389
of the
Criminal Code
.
Dr.
Farrell is no longer in the cabinet, having resigned in August when a Public
Enquiry into his department heard evidence that contracts were let outside the
Public
Tender Act.
On the night before the fire, on April 25, the Opposition
Members tabled documents in the House of Assembly accusing Dr. Farrell and the
Conservative Party with dealing in kickbacks on a multi-million dollar
construction project in St. John's."

(8)
Excerpt from national C.B.C.
television news - September 27, 1978.

"
Jan Tennant
: Last April there
was a fire in the apartment of Dr. Tom Farrell a former Newfoundland cabinet
minister. That fire has been drawing more and more attention from fire experts,
from the police and from opposition politicians who are charging 'cover-up' in
the investigation of the fire. Farrell, the former Minister of Industrial
Development, had been linked by the opposition to an alleged kickback scheme
involving a contractor and Newfoundland's Conservative Party. Paddy Gregg
reports.

"
Paddy Gregg:
Copies of two
police reports have been leaked to the media in St. John's … one, the report of
the initial investigation, has been in the hands of the Department of Justice
since early June, almost four months. It's unequivocal. It contends that Dr.
Farrell set the fire himself and should be charged with arson. The report by
the detective in charge of the investigation ruled out any possibility that the
fire was a result of electrical failure or an inadvertently dropped cigarette.
It also expresses the belief that some highly combustible substance was used to
start the fire. At the time of the fire there had been questions in the House
of Assembly whether documents that might relate to kickback charges had been in
the apartment. There were documents there."

(9)
Excerpt from interview with William
Rowe, leader of the Opposition, by Michael Harris on "Here and Now"
television program on October 4, 1978.

"… it's interesting to note now, that
Premier Moores and Mr. Hickman, and other members of the government, are now
trying to divert attention away from a fire which could have killed scores of
people, including a lot of elderly people in Elizabeth Towers, in trying to
divert attention away from the fact that 5 1/2 months went by before, you know,
the report was finally leaked on the fire which took place without the
government doing anything about it at all, trying to divert attention from the
fire and the possible cover-up and concentrate attention on the leak that took
place. I would say that the least important thing in this case is the actual
leak and the most important thing is that there could have been helpless, innocent,
elderly victims in this case who could have died in that fire, and number two,
that the government gave every appearance of at least dragging its feet and
perhaps trying to perpetrate a cover-up in a very important arson case."

[
9
]

The above are representative samples of what was
carried by the C.B.C. in many news stories during the time period of September
27 to October 5, 1978. Other stories were essentially repeats of the above
quotes.

[
10
]

I turn now to the reasons for judgment of Lang,
J. Having dealt briefly with the facts, the trial judge discussed firstly the
effect of the apology of C.B.C. which, he pointed out, admitted its wrongdoing
only after some four years from the date of commission of the libel. He went on
to say:

"Although I cannot find intentional
express malice, i.e., a deliberate intent to harm Dr. Farrell, I do find
outright carelessness, recklessness and malice on the part of C.B.C. in its
defamation of Dr. Farrell. C.B.C. got what they thought was a juicy scoop (a
blockbuster) when they received the leaked confidential Royal Newfoundland
Constabulary reports and the imagination of those at C.B.C. responsible for its
defamatory broadcasts respecting the plaintiff got the better of them."

[
11
]

He then returned to the effect of the apology
which he felt was of little significance because "C.B.C. kept the matter
going until Dr. Farrell was almost at the courthouse steps". He found that
the sum of $50,000.00 paid into court was not "an appropriate and
reasonable amount in view of the facts of this case" and that Dr. Farrell:

"… was hammered unmercifully for four
years and this hammering injured the plaintiff and no amount of money will
really undo the damage done and therefore a reasonable amount should be awarded
to Dr. Farrell to hopefully alleviate the hardship and injury suffered by the
plaintiff and to show to the public that Dr. Farrell was carelessly and
recklessly wronged (by C.B.C.)."

[
12
]

The trial judge next summarized the evidence in
some detail, which included evidence of Dr. Farrell himself as to the
"disasterous" consequences of the libel, market data as to the
listening and viewing audience of C.B.C. radio and television and evidence from
C.B.C. personnel detailing their reasons for publication which were based
mainly on the authenticity of the reports. The judge also quoted excerpts from
the news reports themselves.

[
13
]

The trial judge as well made numerous references
to an admission by C.B.C. in its apology to the effect that C.B.C. had never
been in possession of any evidence of wrongdoing on the part of Dr. Farrell.
This admission he obviously considered to be aggravating rather than
mitigating.

[
14
]

The law of libel, as well as libel awards in
other Canadian jurisdictions, was next discussed by the trial judge. He then
dealt once more with what he termed were the "devastating results" of
the C.B.C. publications on Dr. Farrell and finding that:

"… C.B.C. acted with malice and acted
carelessly and recklessly with knowledge of the harm it would do to the
plaintiff and his family and if not it should have and ought to have known the
harm the defamatory broadcasts would cause the plaintiff."

and repeating once again much of what he had
already said as to his views of the actions of C.B.C. and the damage caused, he
awarded the sum of $80,000.00 to Dr. Farrell which sum included exemplary as
well as compensatory damages. As seen, he also awarded costs to Dr. Farrell on
a solicitor and "his own" client basis as well as party and party
costs.

[
15
]

Counsel for C.B.C. attacks the judgment
generally, as well as on twelve specific grounds. I do not intend to itemize
each of those grounds here but they will be dealt with, to the extent of their
relevancy, in the course of determining whether or not the award, one of the
highest in monetary terms given in this country, is a proper one in the
circumstances. It should perhaps be noted at this stage that since the filing
of the judgment of Lang, J., the award of Mahoney, J., of $150,000.00 in the
libel actions by Dr. Farrell against the St. John's Evening Telegram has been reduced
by this court to $35,000.00. (See
Thomas Farrell v. St. John's Publishing
Co.
(1985),
1986 CanLII 2436 (NL CA)
, 58 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 66; 174 A.P.R. 66). Leave to appeal to
the Supreme Court of Canada was refused by that court.

[
16
]

Unlike the
Evening Telegram
case, C.B.C.
had acknowledged that a libel was committed by it against Dr. Farrell. It is
therefore unnecessary for me to canvass the law relating to proof of libel
because the fact of defamation of Dr. Farrell's character and/or reputation has
been admitted. In other words, it is conceded (to paraphrase Cave, J., in
Scott
v. Sampson
(1882), 8 Q.B.D. 491
) that the estimation in which Dr. Farrell
stood in the opinion of others was affected by the false statements to his
discredit at the instance of C.B.C. What remains to be determined by this court
is whether the trial judge properly assessed the extent and result of that
infringement.

[
17
]

Libel and slander are of course torts. Thus,
generally speaking, damages arising from the commission of a libel are to be
assessed on a compensatory basis. There must be restitutio in integrum to the
extent that such is possible. This will include damages for pecuniary loss plus
an amount for injury to the plaintiff's feelings and reputation. The latter,
depending on the circumstances of the matter, involve the taking into
consideration of aggravating as well as mitigating factors. Aggravating factors
could include high-handed, malicious, insulting or oppressive behaviour by the
defendant (per Lord Reid in
Cassell v. Broome,
[1972] A.C. 1027
) as well
as failure to apologize and an unsuccessful plea of justification. The extent
of the publication may be, and in this case undoubtedly was, an aggravating
factor.

[
18
]

There may also exist mitigating factors which
could have the effect of reducing the amount of an award, such as the
reputation of the plaintiff, behaviour of the plaintiff toward the defendant
and in the action, any apology tendered by the defendant, other facts
negativing malice on the part of the defendant and sums of money received by
the plaintiff in respect of similar publications.

[
19
]

While the basic principle is compensation, in
certain extraordinary instances exemplary damages may be awarded. An obvious
example is where it is established that the defendant knew he was committing a
tort when he published and decided to publish regardless because the prospect
of material advantage outweighed the prospect of material loss
(Cassell v.
Broome,
supra). As stated by Lord Devlin in
Rookes v. Barnard,
[1964]
A.C. 1129
,

"Exemplary damages can properly be awarded
whenever it is necessary to teach a wrongdoer that tort does not pay."

[
20
]

This brings us to the judgment of Lang, J., and,
specifically, his award of $80,000.00. As has been stated so often that it is
now axiomatic, that award should not be interfered with by this court on appeal
unless it is established that the trial judge acted on some wrong principle of
law or that the amount arrived at is so inordinately high or low as to make it
an entirely erroneous estimate of the damages. This may be determined by an
analysis of the judgment itself and by a comparison of the award with those
given in similar cases.

[
21
]

There can be no doubt that the trial judge did
not err in classifying this as a serious libel. Dr. Farrell was a member of the
Newfoundland Legislature, maintaining quite a high profile, having been, up to
a few weeks prior to the fire, Minister of Public Works in the Cabinet of then
Premier Moores. It was unquestionably the fact of this high profile which
induced C.B.C. (and others) to give extensive publicity to what the trial judge
characterized as a "blockbuster" story. The C.B.C. obviously was
willing to take the chance of equating the authenticity of the police reports
with the veracity of the allegations contained therein for the purpose of
publicizing that "blockbuster" story.

[
22
]

Other publications notwithstanding, C.B.C.
through its radio and television outlets reached all households within the
Province and the extent of that coverage is verified in the evidence.
Television in particular is a very powerful medium and the nature of the
coverage given the story by a communicator as prominent as the C.B.C., not only
within the Province but nationally as well, cannot be overstated. C.B.C.
further, through interviews and its own commentary, conveyed the impression to
its viewers and listeners not only that the fire had been started by Dr.
Farrell but that it had been done deliberately, that it had been done for the
possible purpose of concealing damaging Government documents and that the
result of the fire could have been the deaths of many persons in the apartment
building. It does not matter that this method of getting rid of documents is
totally illogical or that bodily injury or death was an unlikely result of this
particular fire. That was the imprint left by the stories. There was also
suggestion of a Government "cover-up" of the matter in which Dr.
Farrell was presumably involved.

[
23
]

Strictly speaking, no special damages were
proved inasmuch as no evidence was adduced of actual pecuniary loss to Dr. Farrell.
However, while it is obviously impossible to quantify in strict terms the
pecuniary loss to Dr. Farrell resulting from the stories, there can be no doubt
that they had to be extremely stressful to him personally and that his
character and reputation were adversely affected. Further, it is difficult to
conceive that this injury to his reputation did not result in some pecuniary
loss. For this combination of economic and noneconomic loss, a substantial
award against C.B.C. is unquestionably warranted.

[
24
]

The award of $80,000.00 is, however, not only
substantial, it is very high. In reaching that figure, the trial judge was most
likely influenced by the award of Mahoney, J., in the
Evening Telegram
case,
but additionally he appears, with respect, to have reached unwarranted
conclusions from certain parts of the evidence and to have misconstrued other
aspects of that evidence. There are further mitigating factors to which he
appears not to have turned his mind.

[
25
]

The trial judge appears to ascribe the delay in
bringing the matter to trial totally to C.B.C. and that the result of that
delay was that Dr. Farrell was "hammered unmercifully for four years"
(by C.B.C.). This statement is not justified on the evidence. The offensive
statements were published over a five day period up to October 5, 1978. Dr.
Farrell was charged with arson on October 20, 1978. He was discharged on
December 18, 1978 and certainly, if not by that date, then by the time Judge
LeClair filed his written reasons for the discharge, Dr. Farrell would have
been seen to be vindicated. If any odour of suspicion hung to Dr. Farrell after
that time, there is no evidence that it caused any further damage to him.
Further, it was up to him and his solicitors to bring the matter on for trial.
Instead, the
Evening Telegram
action was brought on first and this
action obviously awaited the outcome of that trial.

[
26
]

No delay can be ascribed to C.B.C., nor any
"unmerciful hammering" of Dr. Farrell as the result of any delay.
There is no justification for that statement. Further, if the trial judge is
suggesting that the total effect on the respondent resulted from what C.B.C.
did, this is obviously overstated. To repeat, the published libels continued
only over a five day period. Much of the effect on Dr. Farrell after that time
was the result of the fire itself and the ensuing criminal charge. The libels
published by the C.B.C. (and the Evening Telegram) certainly had some
considerable effect, but the whole damage to the respondent cannot be ascribed
to them.

[
27
]

The learned trial judge likewise placed great
import on the fact that the apology which preceded the consent judgment and
payment into court of $50,000.00 contained a statement that C.B.C. did not
have, and never had, any evidence of wrongdoing by Dr. Farrell. This is
mentioned on numerous occasions and treated by the judge as a highly
aggravating factor. To put it in perspective, however, it is only an
unequivocal apology in a form demanded by Dr. Farrell's solicitors, which
demand was acceded to (done, one surmises, after the verdict in the
Evening
Telegram
trials which would have left C.B.C. with little doubt as to where
it stood). I do not consider the apology to be a mitigating factor, as
suggested by counsel for C.B.C., because of its lateness in coming, but it is
certainly not a factor of aggravation. The plea of justification contained in
the defence was an aggravation, but the fact that such defence remained on the
court record prior to trial and during settlement negotiations cannot be
construed heavily against C.B.C. as it would be if pursued at trial.

[
28
]

There are various other comments made by the
trial judge, e.g., that the broadcasts "destroyed" Dr. Farrell and
that he was ruined professionally and politically as a result of the actions of
C.B.C. These cannot be substantiated and, in fact, appear to be contrary to the
evidence.

[
29
]

The trial judge found that there was no
deliberate intention on the part of C.B.C. to injure Dr. Farrell, but that
there was "outright carelessness, recklessness and malice" by C.B.C.
I do not quarrel with the judge's finding of carelessness and recklessness up
to a point, but it is clear from the judgment as a whole that the trial judge
accepted the evidence of Dr. Farrell in toto and, to a great extent,
disregarded that of the defence. In doing so, he in my view overlooked certain
factors which should have had a mitigating effect on the amount of damages
awarded.

[
30
]

For example, other than the malice which must be
presumed to sustain a defamation action, the evidence indicates that there was
no express or actual malice on the part of C.B.C. There was no antagonism
toward Dr. Farrell, nor any improper motive. The libel was careless and
reckless, but obviously published because, as stated above, C.B.C. equated the
authenticity of the reports with their truthfulness. This does not justify the
libel in any way, but does demonstrate the absence of malice. Further, the fact
of the charge being laid and the lack of evidence as to continuing damage to
Dr. Farrell are all factors going to mitigation which appear to have been
overlooked by the trial judge.

[
31
]

Finally, in the matter of quantum, it is
necessary to consider other awards. It is these which demonstrate that, despite
the nature of C.B.C.'s actions in this matter, and in the absence of proved
pecuniary loss, the trial judge's award is clearly excessive.

[
32
]

There are five relatively recent cases which, in
my opinion, put this matter in its right perspective. These are: (1)
Baxter
v. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and Mailing
(1980),
1980 CanLII 3195 (NB CA)
, 30 N.B.R.(2d) 102;
70 A.P.R. 102; (2)
Snyder v. Montreal Gazette
(1983),
1983 CanLII 2859 (QC CA)
, 5 D.L.R.(4th) 206;
(3)
Vogel v. Canadian Broadcasting Corporation et al.,
1982 CanLII 801 (BC SC)
, [1982] 3 W.W.R.
97; (4)
Munro v. Toronto Sun Publishing Corporation
(1982),
1982 CanLII 1758 (ON HCJ)
, 39 O.R. (2d)
100; and (5)
Farrell v. St. John's Publishing Co.
,
supra.

[
33
]

The
Baxter

case bears some minor
resemblance to the case at bar. The plaintiff sued in libel for having been
defamed on the C.B.C. program "The Fifth Estate" which stated that
when he was New Brunswick Minister of Justice, he stopped an investigation by
the R.C.M.P. into alleged "kickbacks" to a Conservative Party fund.
On appeal, an award of $1,000.00 given at trial was increased to $10,000.00.
There was no imputation of criminal conduct and there was only one broadcast
item. In
Snyder
,
a trial jury had awarded the plaintiff $135,000.00
because of an article in the
Gazette
which published an article
concerning the plaintiff, a prominent public figure, which article was headed
"Former City Official called member of 'Jewish Mafia'". On appeal, by
a 2-1 majority, the award was reduced, rather spectacularly, to $13,-500.00
which, the majority felt, represented the
Gazette's
share of the total
damage to Mr. Snyder, severe pecuniary damages not having been proved. (This
case is under appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.)

[
34
]

In
Vogel

and
Munro
(both of which
are dealt with extensively in the judgment of Morgan, J.A., of this court in
the
Farrell v. Evening Telegram
case [see (1986),
1986 CanLII 2436 (NL CA)
, 58 Nfld. &
P.E.I.R. 66; 174 A.P.R. 66]), a provincial Deputy Attorney General and a
federal cabinet minister were seriously libelled. In the former case, it was
reported that Mr. Vogel had interfered with the course of justice in three
criminal trials to protect friends and, in the latter, an article was published
stating that Mr. Munro had used information given to him in cabinet meetings to
make profits for himself and for another person by the timely purchase of
Petrofina shares. The awards were $125,000.00 and $75,000.00 respectively.
However, as already pointed out by Mr. Justice Morgan, these cases involved
exemplary or punitive damages, which I feel are not called for here, in
addition to compensatory damages and were much more serious than the present
case because, as stated by him (at page 82):

"These cases differ from the case at bar
in that, in both, the defendants were the originators of the libellous
publications. In
Vogel
,
the defendants were found to be motivated by a
desire for sensationalism and broadcast the defamatory story in reckless
disregard for any injury that would be occasioned the plaintiff. In
Munro

the
libellous article was published out of personal spite. In both, the need for an
award of punitive damages was apparent."

[
35
]

There are of course many other examples, but the
above are all recent cases of serious libels, the awards for which represent
the accepted range in terms of money adopted by Canadian courts. These awards
demonstrate that despite our acquiescence generally with the trial judge's
characterization of the actions of C.B.C. and their effect on Dr. Farrell, the
award of $80,000.00 is inordinately high.

[
36
]

However, the authority which must guide this
court in its arriving at a proper award is the' court's judgment in
Farrell
v. St. John's Publishing Co.
,
supra. The total award in that case was
reduced from $150,000.00 to $35,000.00 which figure must be accepted as being
the appropriate one on its facts. Inasmuch as the present matter arises out of
the same set of circumstances, the nature and effect of the libel in the
Telegram

case must be compared with this one. If this libel was more serious, the
award should be higher. If not, it should not.

[
37
]

The
Telegram
libel was published in its
daily newspaper on several occasions. The newspaper is extensively read on the
Avalon Peninsula, but has relatively limited circulation, except in the larger
urban centres, outside the Avalon. The nature and extent of the C.B.C. coverage
has already been discussed above and there can be no doubt that the defamation
reached many more persons than did the
Telegram
libel and, because of
the nature of the medium, had a more profound and lasting effect on them; This
fact, together with the manner in which the material was presented, had of
necessity in my view to cause more damage to Dr. Farrell than the
Telegram
stories.
A higher award is therefore warranted.

[
38
]

As
in the
Telegram

case, we are dealing here with aggravated compensatory damages, but, for
the reasons stated above, not with exemplary damages as found by the trial
judge. As seen, there was no deliberate attempt to injure or reprehensible
conduct which could be termed actual or express malice or, for that matter,
anything else which would justify the award of exemplary damages. The damages
are nevertheless - aggravated, not only by the method of presentation of some
of the reports, but they must also reflect the court's condemnation of what can
only be termed moral irresponsibility on the part of a respected corporation
acknowledged to be a leader in its field and whose statements are normally
given great weight by its listeners and viewers. The C.B.C. not only committed
a serious libel by the publishing of the contents of reports "leaked"
to it, but the reports in question were obtained by improper means and that
fact was known by C.B.C.

[
39
]

In the result, and in the circumstances, it is
my view that an award of damages of $45,000.00 would adequately satisfy the
above referred-to considerations and I would vary the judgment accordingly.
Monies paid in respect of the principal sum paid by C.B.C. to Dr. Farrell will
be repaid.

[
40
]

It follows obviously from the above that the
respondent's cross-appeal must fail. It is further obvious that, Dr. Farrell
having obtained less by way of judgment than the $50,000.00 paid into court by
C.B.C., the latter should not have been put to the expense of trial. Therefore,
as to costs at the trial level, Dr. Farrell will have his costs to the date of
payment into court of the $50,000.00, and the C.B.C. will have its costs
thereafter. C.B.C. is also entitled to the costs of the appeal. All costs shall
be on a party and party basis.

[
41
]

It is also apparent that it is not necessary to
consider the appeal of C.B.C. as to the awarding of solicitor and "his
own" client costs. That issue will have to await a more appropriate time.

[
42
]

In the result, it is ordered that:

A. The amount of damages awarded to the
respondent be reduced to $45,-000.00;

B. The order of the trial judge as to costs
be set aside;

C. The respondent recover against the
appellant his costs on a party and party basis to the time of payment into
court, to be taxed;

D. The appellant recover against the
respondent its costs on a party and party basis from the time of payment in,
and on appeal, to be taxed; and

E. The respondent repay to the appellant the
amount of money which he has received pursuant to the trial judgment in excess
of his entitlement pursuant to this judgment.

……………………………………………………………………………………….

[
43
]

Goodridge, C.J.N.: I have read the decision of'
Gushue, J.A., in this matter and concur with it. I wish only to add a few
observations of my own.

[
44
]

There has been a tendency in libel actions to
assume that large sums of money should be awarded. Such a tendency has probably
developed, because of the relatively substantial awards that have been made in
England and in the United States. While a libel is in no sense to be condoned
there is generally little justification for extravagant awards. As Mr. Justice
Gushue pointed out libel is a tort and the damages awarded are by way of
compensation.

[
45
]

In Canada there have been very few cases where
awards have exceeded $50,-000.00. Most of these involved allowances for
exemplary damages.

[
46
]

In most tort actions, damages consist of special
damages and general damages.

[
47
]

Special damages are those which are capable of
being specially pleaded and specifically proved. General damages are usually
divided into those sums which represent economic loss and those sums which
represent noneconomic loss.

[
48
]

In actions for defamation, the approach to the
assessment of damages is different.

[
49
]

The term "special damage" occurs,
primarily with reference to actions for slander for no such action lies without
proof of special damage. In the context of defamation, special damage includes
special damages and general damages consisting of economic loss.

[
50
]

There are unlikely to be special damages in
actions for defamation. What the term special damage probably means is material
loss, a term suggested by Lord Hailsham of St. Marylebone, L.C., in
Broome
v. Cassell,
[1972] A.C. 1027
. That would be synonymous with special damages
and general damages consisting of economic loss.

[
51
]

Damages other than for material loss are termed
"damages at large". These have been variously defined but appear
generally to mean general damages consisting of noneconomic loss and exemplary
damages in appropriate cases.

[
52
]

Lord Hailsham of St. Marylebone in
Broome v.
Cassell
suggested as follows at page 1073:

"The expression 'at large' should be
used in general to cover all cases where awards of damages may include elements
for loss of reputation, injured feelings, bad or good conduct by either party,
or punishment, and where in consequence no precise limit can be set."

[
53
]

Because they include compensation for loss of
reputation, damages at large probably encompasses economic loss that can be
foreseen but not readily quantified.

[
54
]

The components of the award in defamation cases
are compensatory and exemplary damages. There may be factors aggravating or
mitigating the first component so that it may be greater or less than it might
otherwise be.

[
55
]

Exemplary damages are awarded in circumstances
where the conduct of the defendant merits punishment. Such conduct has been
described in a variety of ways, ranging from deliberate conduct calculated to
harm to reprehensible and irresponsible conduct.

[
56
]

Whether the concept of exemplary damages is one
that should continue as it is now considered to exist in Canada or should be
confined as it has been in England (see
Rookes v. Barnard,
[1964] A.C.
1129 (H.L.)
) is a matter for another day.

[
57
]

The amount awarded for damages at large is
usually expressed as a global figure although, occasionally, a separate figure
for exemplary damages is stated.

[
58
]

There has been a tendency in some cases to
compare the amount allowed in damage awards for libel with the amount of
$100,000.00 which in 1978 the Supreme Court of Canada in the trilogy of cases
beginning with
Andrews v. Grand and Toy (Alberta) Ltd.,
1978 CanLII 1 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R.
229; [1978] 1 W.W.R. 557; 19 N.R. 50; 8 A.R. 182; 83 D.L.R.(3d) 452; 3 C.C.L.T.
225, suggested was the most that should be allowed for noneconomic loss in
cases of personal injury. The question arises as to whether that limitation
extends to actions for defamation. Whether it does or not, some degree of
restraint must be exercised. A man's damaged reputation may be restored; lost
limbs cannot be replaced.

[
59
]

Damage awards should reflect the economic loss
of the plaintiff to the extent that it is capable of calculation and the
damages at large. There is no way to assess the damages at large by reference
to the parties and the libel only. There must be reference to and comparison
with other decided cases. The circumstances of a case under consideration may
be assessed as more serious than one, less so than another, and thereby a
figure will be indicated. Dollar amounts in earlier cases should be restated in
current values for true comparisons.

[
60
]

The goal is predictability. Widespread
inconsistencies create uncertainties.

[
61
]

In a case of a professional person such as Dr.
Farrell it may be possible to establish by a comparison of prelibel and
post-libel income that there was a real economic loss. There was no evidence
before the court that Dr. Farrell suffered a quantifiable economic loss as a
result of the C.B.C. libel against him.

[
62
]

In considering the damages at large, there must
be brought into balance all of the other factors which troubled Dr. Farrell at
the time. There was the fact of the fire itself of course. Dr. Farrell was
charged with arson but he was not committed for trial. There were also the
Soper and Legrow inquiries and the consultation with Hon. R.S. Furlong.

[
63
]

Moreover, there was the libel of the
Evening
Telegram
for which Dr. Farrell received $35,000.00. It was correctly argued
that C.B.C. is not entitled to offset against its liability to Dr. Farrell the
amount that was recovered by him in a separate libel action against another
tortfeasor. Nevertheless, C.B.C. is only liable for the damages which it caused
(and exemplary damages' if applicable).

[
64
]

To the extent that Dr. Farrell's troubles were
caused by the appellant, the appellant is answerable.

[
65
]

There are no significant mitigating factors
present here. There was a degree of aggravation. The measure of damages is
largely influenced by the eloquence with which the libel may be described.
There is no doubt that Dr. Farrell was grievously libelled. The extent to which
the libel was aggravated is not as extensive as the trial judge has suggested.
The libel itself was published over a period of five days. C.B.C. maintained a
plea of justification over a period of four years but at the time of trial
admitted its liability and paid into court $50,000.00. Maintaining a plea of
justification is an aggravating circumstance.

[
66
]

Upon an overview of the award I agree that the
amount allowed by the trial judge is far in excess of the amount of
compensation to which Dr. Farrell is entitled and that the award should be
reduced to $45,000.00. The libel here is of greater dimension than the
Evening
Telegram
libel.

[
67
]

With regard to costs the trial judge allowed
party and party costs and solicitor and his own client costs.

[
68
]

An award of solicitor and his own client costs
seems to be based on the concept that the successful victim of a libel should
recover not only the damage award but also his reasonable legal fees and
expenses reasonably incurred. While there may be justification for the
proposition that any tort victim should be entitled not only to recover his
damages but also the cost of recovering those damages, that has not been
accepted as a principle of law at this time. There appears to be no
justification for making such an allowance in isolated libel cases.

[
69
]

The term "solicitor and his own
client" apparently arises under the English rules providing for taxation
of a solicitor's bill to his client. The term "costs on an indemnity
basis" is probably preferable, meaning indemnity to the successful party
for all costs reasonably incurred and reasonable as to amount. (See
EMI
Records v. Wallace,
[1982] 2 All E.R. 980
.)

[
70
]

I agree with the disposition of this appeal in
the manner outlined by Mr. Justice Gushue. Appeal allowed.
